title: Matthew 8:5–13
context: In Capernaum a Roman centurion appeals for a paralyzed servant. His insight into authority draws Jesus’ marvel and opens a window onto Gentile inclusion and the danger of covenant presumption—faith that trusts the word, not proximity or pedigree.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 8:5–13.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: There came to him a centurion - A captain of a hundred Roman soldiers. Probably he came a little way toward him, and then went back. He thought himself not worthy to come in person, and therefore spoke the words that follow by his messengers.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 8:5–13)

reformed.quote: And when Jesus had entered Those who think that Matthew and Luke give different narratives, are led into a mistake by a mere trifle. The only difference in the words is, that Matthew says that the centurion came to him, while Luke says that he sent some of the Jews to plead in his name.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 8:5–13)

verses.text: When he came into Capernaum, a centurion came to him, asking him for help,
verses.arminianNotes:
Capernaum receives a Gentile officer who comes forward and appeals. Empire’s rank does not bar approach; need and humility do the talking.

Arminian readers see grace widening the circle. The centurion is not chased away; he is heard. Responsibility remains: he must actually come and ask.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew places a centurion inside Jesus’ Capernaum ministry. Gentile faith will soon be praised above Israel’s average response—already under the story God is writing.

The Lord of Israel draws a Roman soldier near at the appointed hour, preparing the theme of east-and-west guests at the kingdom table.

verses.text: saying, “Lord, my servant lies in the house paralyzed, grievously tormented.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The plea is concrete and compassionate: a servant paralyzed and suffering. Authority here bends toward the weak.

Faith often begins with love for another’s pain. Grace enables intercession; the centurion uses his voice for someone who cannot walk to Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Lord” on a Gentile tongue already signals more than courtesy. The description is stark—paralyzed, suffering terribly.

Christ receives petitions for the helpless. The servant’s misery is not beneath the King’s notice; this need will showcase faith and authority together.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus answers with readiness: He will come and heal. Willingness meets the appeal without delay or disdain.

Wesleyan Arminians hear a Savior eager to help. The offer to come is sincere; grace does not play hard to get when true need is presented.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King’s “I will come” shows initiative. Healing is not bargained; it is granted from sovereign kindness.

Christ’s resolve to heal stands before the centurion’s famous reply. Mercy originates in Jesus, not in human negotiation.

verses.text: The centurion answered, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Unworthiness and confidence sit together: not worthy of a visit, yet sure that a word is enough. Faith grasps distance-bridging authority.

This is living trust—humble about self, bold about Christ. Grace enables such insight; the man freely confesses both need and Jesus’ power.
verses.reformedNotes:
The centurion refuses presumption. Roof-worthiness is denied; word-sufficiency is affirmed. That is the anatomy of true faith.

Such humility and confidence are gifts. He sees that Christ’s spoken will is as effective as His bodily presence—authority that creates what it commands.
verses.keyContrast: Both celebrate humble, word-trusting faith. Arminians underline the centurion’s responsible insight and plea under assisting grace; Calvinists stress faith as Spirit-wrought gift that rests wholly on Christ’s efficacious word.

verses.text: For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and tell another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and tell my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Military chain-of-command becomes a parable of Jesus’ power. Orders work at a distance; so, he reasons, must the Lord’s word.

Arminian interpreters admire clear-eyed reasoning in faith. Light given is used well. The centurion thinks truly about authority and then trusts accordingly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Analogy from barracks to kingdom: delegated command implies greater command in the Commander. The centurion’s logic is theological.

God has granted unusual clarity. This Gentile perceives what many near the covenant signs miss—Jesus’ word carries irresistible authority.

verses.text: When Jesus heard it, he marveled and said to those who followed, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus marvels—and Israel is put on notice. Covenant nearness without trust is empty; a Gentile’s faith can outshine privileged hearers.

Arminian pastoral warning and hope: privilege does not save; faith does. Grace was offered widely in Israel; many resisted. This centurion shows what receptive faith looks like.
verses.reformedNotes:
Divine marvel is true in the narrative: Jesus highlights faith rare even in Israel. Election’s surprise is already visible—outsiders believing, insiders missing.

Finding such faith “I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel” judges presumption. God raises faith where He wills; pedigree is no substitute for trusting Christ’s word.
verses.keyContrast: Both take Jesus’ marvel as rebuke to covenant presumption and praise of Gentile faith. Arminians highlight Israel’s genuine opportunity refused and the centurion’s receptive response; Calvinists emphasize God’s freedom to grant faith beyond ethnic Israel and expose empty privilege.

verses.text: I tell you that many will come from the east and the west, and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven,
verses.arminianNotes:
East and west guests at the patriarchs’ table: the kingdom’s feast is wider than ethnic Israel imagined. Faith, not bloodline, seats the diner.

Classical Arminians rejoice in global gospel invitation. Many will come—inclusion for those who believe. Abraham’s family grows by faith’s welcome.
verses.reformedNotes:
Promise to Abraham expands in Jesus’ mouth: nations stream to the kingdom banquet. The patriarchs’ table is secured by God’s covenant purpose.

Gentile inclusion is not Plan B. The very Lord who called Abraham now gathers east and west according to electing mercy fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: but the children of the Kingdom will be thrown out into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Sons of the kingdom face outer darkness if they refuse the King’s faith-call. Nearness without trust ends in weeping.

Privilege heightens responsibility. Grace was near; rejection is culpable. The warning aims to awaken, not to entertain despair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Judgment language is stark: outer darkness, weeping, gnashing. Covenant labels do not cancel unbelief’s end.

God’s justice is not sentimental. Those who presume on lineage while rejecting the Messiah meet the judgment Scripture names—under the same sovereign hand that seats Gentiles at the feast.
verses.keyContrast: Both preach actual judgment on unbelieving privilege. Arminians typically underline culpable refusal of near grace; Reformed readers underline judicial outcome under God’s righteous decree against unbelief, even among “children of the Kingdom.”

verses.text: Jesus said to the centurion, “Go your way. Let it be done for you as you have believed.” His servant was healed in that hour.
verses.arminianNotes:
“As you have believed” ties the gift to living trust; healing arrives that very moment. Faith receives what it entrusted to Jesus’ word.

Believe and go. The centurion’s trust was not empty; grace answered. Believers today are summoned to the same word-dependent confidence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Authority speaks: “let it be done.” Belief is the appointed instrument; Christ is the efficient cause. Instant healing seals the lesson.

Faith does not create power; it rests on power already present in Jesus. The servant’s cure proves the word sufficient and the King faithful.
verses.keyContrast: Both join faith and healing without making faith a human merit. Arminians typically present believing as the grace-enabled condition that receives; Reformed readers typically present faith as the Spirit-given instrument through which Christ’s sovereign word heals.
